lessons.title: What it actually is
lessons.summary: Pattern-matching at enormous scale — not understanding, not magic, and not a person.
objectives: You will explain prediction from patterns in your own words
You will name three things these systems do well
You will name three they do badly
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play a prediction game: the class guesses the next word in a sentence
- Discuss what the system is actually doing — statistics over examples
- List what it is good at and bad at

## Understand it

The AI tools you hear about — chatbots, image generators, voice assistants — are built on **machine learning**: instead of a programmer writing every rule, the system is shown millions of examples and adjusts itself until its outputs match them.

A chatbot's core job is surprisingly simple to describe: **predict the next word**. Given "The sun rises in the…", it has seen enough text to rate "east" as very likely. Do that once, add the word, predict again, and repeat hundreds of times, and you get paragraphs. The prediction is done by a **model** — a huge set of numbers (parameters) tuned during **training** on enormous amounts of text.

That explains a lot:

- It is **fluent**, because it learnt from fluent text.
- It has **no understanding or intentions** in the way a person does. It does not know whether what it writes is true; it knows what is likely to come next.
- It reflects its **training data** — including its gaps and its prejudices.
- It can be **very useful** for drafting, summarising, explaining and brainstorming, as long as a person checks the result.

The word "intelligence" is marketing as much as description. A clearer phrase is *pattern-matching at enormous scale*. Keep that in mind and you will use these tools well: as fast, tireless assistants that need a human to check their work.

## Key words

- **Machine learning:** computers learning patterns from examples instead of following hand-written rules
- **Model:** the trained system that makes predictions
- **Training data:** the examples a model learns from
- **Prediction:** the model's best guess of what comes next

## Read and watch

- [Elements of AI](https://www.elementsofai.com/) — University of Helsinki
- [How AI works](https://code.org/ai) — Code.org
- [Policy guidance on AI for children](https://www.unicef.org/innocenti/reports/policy-guidance-ai-children) — UNICEF

## Practise at home

1. Explain to someone at home what these systems are, without the word "magic"
1. Write down one thing you expected it could do that it cannot

lessons.title: Training data, and where bias comes from
lessons.summary: A model learns from examples, so whatever is skewed in the examples is skewed in the model.
objectives: You will say where training data comes from
You will predict a bias from a described dataset
You will test a real system for one bias
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Build a tiny dataset as a class and notice what it leaves out
- Predict: if a dataset has few Nigerian examples, what will the model be bad at?
- Test an image generator or search for a role and see who it shows

## Understand it

A model can only learn from the examples it is given. If the examples are skewed, the model is skewed — and it applies that skew to thousands of people, quickly and without noticing.

Bias gets in several ways:

- **Who is in the data.** If a face-recognition system is trained mostly on light-skinned faces, it will make more mistakes on darker-skinned faces. Researchers have measured exactly this in commercial systems.
- **What the past looked like.** A hiring model trained on ten years of a company's decisions learns whatever unfairness those decisions contained.
- **How the data was labelled.** People label examples, and people bring their assumptions.
- **What is missing.** Languages, accents and places with less internet text — including many Nigerian languages — are poorly represented, so tools work worse for them.

Bias is not usually anybody's intention, which is exactly why it is dangerous: nobody notices unless they test for it. Good practice is to ask, before trusting a system: *Who was in the training data? Who is missing? Has it been tested on people like the ones it will be used on — and how often does it fail for each group?*

The fix is never only technical. It needs diverse teams, better data, testing by group, and humans who can override the machine.

## Key words

- **Bias:** a systematic unfairness in results, often for one group
- **Representative data:** examples that include all the kinds of people a system will meet
- **Label:** the answer attached to a training example

## Read and watch

- [Gender Shades: intersectional accuracy disparities (the research paper)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v81/buolamwini18a.html) — Proceedings of Machine Learning Research
- [Algorithmic Justice League](https://www.ajl.org/) — Algorithmic Justice League
- [Elements of AI](https://www.elementsofai.com/) — University of Helsinki

1. Write one sentence on who was missing from its answers

lessons.title: Asking well, and checking
lessons.summary: A clear prompt, and the verification step that makes the answer usable.
objectives: You will write a prompt with role, task, context and format
You will verify an answer against a source
You will say why an unverified answer is not an answer
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Write a vague prompt and a precise one; compare the answers
- Take one factual claim from the answer and check it against a real source
- Record what you asked, what it said, how you checked

## Understand it

A prompt is an instruction. The clearer it is, the more useful the answer. A good prompt usually includes:

- **The task** — what you want: explain, summarise, list, rewrite, suggest.
- **The context** — who it is for and what you already know: "I am 13 and new to fractions".
- **The format** — "in five bullet points", "in under 100 words", "as a table".
- **Constraints** — "use Nigerian examples", "do not use technical words".

Compare "Tell me about photosynthesis" with "Explain photosynthesis to a 13-year-old in five short steps, with one everyday example, and end with a question I can test myself on." The second is far more useful.

Then comes the step most people skip: **checking**. These tools can be wrong while sounding certain. For anything that matters:

1. **Check facts** against a reliable source — a textbook, an official site, a teacher.
2. **Check reasoning** — does each step actually follow?
3. **Check fit** — does it answer *your* question, for *your* situation?
4. **Ask it to show its working**, or to give sources — then check those sources exist; it can invent them.

An answer you have checked is useful. An answer you have not checked is a guess with good grammar.

## Key words

- **Prompt:** the instruction you give the system
- **Context:** background information that shapes a useful answer
- **Verification:** checking an answer against reliable sources

## Read and watch

- [Elements of AI](https://www.elementsofai.com/) — University of Helsinki
- [SIFT: checking information](https://hapgood.us/2019/06/19/sift-the-four-moves/) — Mike Caulfield

1. Keep the log: asked, answered, checked

lessons.title: Confidently wrong
lessons.summary: Hallucination: why the system invents things, and why it sounds just as sure when it does.
objectives: You will make a system state something false
You will say why confidence is not accuracy
You will name two topics where you should never trust it unchecked
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Ask about an obscure local fact and check the answer
- Ask it for a book or a law that does not exist, and watch it invent one
- List the topics where being wrong is dangerous: medicine, law, money, people

## Understand it

A **hallucination** is when an AI system produces something false — a made-up fact, quote, statistic, book or website — and presents it with the same confidence as the truth.

Why does it happen? Because the model is predicting likely words, not looking facts up. If you ask for "three studies on Lagos traffic", it knows what a study citation *looks like* — author, year, title, journal — and can produce convincing ones that do not exist. There is no internal alarm that says "I don't actually know this".

Hallucinations are most likely when:

- the question is about something **rare, local or recent** (your school, your street, last week's news);
- you ask for **specifics** — exact numbers, dates, names, references, quotes;
- the question **assumes something false** ("Why did Lagos become Nigeria's capital in 2010?") and the model plays along.

How to protect yourself:

- Treat every specific claim as unverified until you have checked it elsewhere.
- Search for any book, article or link it gives you. If you cannot find it, it is probably invented.
- Ask "How sure are you, and how could I check?" — but remember the answer to that can be wrong too.
- Use these tools for things you can judge yourself — drafting, explaining a concept you can test — rather than for facts you cannot verify.

## Key words

- **Hallucination:** a confident but false output from an AI system
- **Fabricated citation:** a reference to a source that does not exist
- **False premise:** a question built on something untrue

## Read and watch

- [How to fact check](https://fullfact.org/toolkit/) — Full Fact
- [News Literacy Project](https://newslit.org/) — News Literacy Project

1. Write down what gave it away

lessons.title: Machine learning on paper
lessons.summary: Classifying by hand, so you can see exactly what a model is doing.
objectives: You will classify examples by hand using rules you choose
You will measure your accuracy
You will improve the rules and measure again
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Sort 20 written examples into two classes using a rule you write
- Count how many you got right
- Change the rule and count again

## Understand it

You can do machine learning with a pencil. Suppose you want to sort fruit into **mangoes** and **oranges** using two **features**: weight and how smooth the skin is. Plot ten fruits you already know on a graph — weight across, smoothness up. The mangoes cluster in one area, the oranges in another. Draw a line between the groups. Now a new fruit arrives: measure it, plot it, and see which side of the line it falls. You have just built a **classifier**.

That is essentially what a computer does, with many more features and examples:

1. **Training data** — examples with known labels ("this is a mango").
2. **Features** — the measurable things it uses to decide.
3. **Learning** — finding the boundary that best separates the labels.
4. **Prediction** — placing new, unlabelled examples.

Notice the weaknesses you can see on paper:

- A fruit near the line is a **guess**; the model will still give a confident answer.
- If your training examples were all small mangoes, a big mango may be called an orange — the model only knows what it was shown.
- If you chose bad features (colour, when both are green and orange), no line separates them well.

We test a model on examples it has **not** seen during training, and count how often it is right. Testing on the training examples would be like marking an exam with the answers you were taught.

## Key words

- **Classifier:** a model that sorts things into categories
- **Feature:** a measurable property used to decide, like weight
- **Decision boundary:** the line that separates categories
- **Test set:** examples kept back to check how well a model works

## Read and watch

- [Teachable Machine](https://teachablemachine.withgoogle.com/) — Google
- [Elements of AI](https://www.elementsofai.com/) — University of Helsinki

1. Record both accuracy scores

lessons.title: Images, voices and deepfakes
lessons.summary: Generated media, how to spot it, and what it means for trusting what you see.
objectives: You will identify three signs of a generated image
You will say why voice cloning is dangerous
You will name what to do if someone uses your likeness
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Look at generated images and find the tells: hands, text, edges, background
- Discuss voice cloning scams — a relative calls asking for money
- Agree a family code word as a defence

## Understand it

Generative systems can now make realistic images, voices and video of things that never happened. A **deepfake** is synthetic media that shows a real person doing or saying something they never did.

This matters because pictures and voices used to be evidence. A fake voice note "from your uncle" asking for money, a fake video of a politician, a fake photo of a classmate — each can do real harm, and they are cheap to make.

Clues that something may be generated (though the best fakes may show none):

- **Hands, teeth, ears and jewellery** that look odd or melt into each other.
- **Text** in the image that is garbled.
- **Lighting and shadows** that do not match.
- In video: **blinking, lip-sync** or edges around the face that flicker.
- In voice: flat emotion, odd breathing, or a request that is urgent and secret.

Because detection by eye is getting harder, the stronger habits are about **context**: Who posted it first? Is it reported by reliable sources? Does the person's official account confirm it? For a voice note asking for money or secrets, **call the person back on a number you already have**.

And the rule for creators: never make or share fake media of a real person, and label anything you generate.

## Key words

- **Synthetic media:** images, audio or video made by software rather than recorded
- **Deepfake:** synthetic media showing a real person doing something they never did
- **Provenance:** where a piece of media came from and how it was made

## Read and watch

- [News Literacy Project](https://newslit.org/) — News Literacy Project

lessons.title: Bias again, with a real case
lessons.summary: Returning to week 2 with a documented real-world failure, and what should have been done.
objectives: You will study a real documented bias failure
You will connect it to the week 2 dataset exercise
You will say what would have caught it
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Study one documented case of a biased system causing harm
- Trace it back to the training data
- Say what test would have caught it before release

## Understand it

Real cases show how bias causes harm — and what should have been done. Two well-documented examples:

**Hiring.** A large technology company built a system to rank job applicants by learning from ten years of past CVs. Most past hires in technical roles had been men, so the system learnt to mark down CVs containing words associated with women, such as "women's chess club". The company found the problem and abandoned the tool.

**Face analysis.** Researchers at MIT (the *Gender Shades* study) tested commercial systems that guess gender from faces. They were almost always right for lighter-skinned men and wrong far more often for darker-skinned women — because those faces were under-represented in the data used to build and test them.

What should have happened, in both cases:

1. **Ask who could be harmed** before building.
2. **Check the data** for who is missing or over-represented.
3. **Test results separately for each group**, not only the overall accuracy — a system can be "95% accurate" overall and fail badly for one group.
4. **Keep a human in charge** of decisions that affect people's lives, with a way to appeal.
5. **Publish** how the system was tested.

Return to your week 2 notes: which of these steps would have caught the problems you discussed then?

## Key words

- **Disaggregated testing:** measuring accuracy separately for each group
- **Human oversight:** a person who can check and overrule an automated decision
- **Accountability:** being answerable for what a system does

## Read and watch

- [Gender Shades: intersectional accuracy disparities (the research paper)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v81/buolamwini18a.html) — Proceedings of Machine Learning Research

lessons.title: What you must never put in
lessons.summary: Privacy: what happens to what you type, and the things that must not go in the box.
objectives: You will list what must never be entered
You will say what happens to what you type
You will find and read one tool's data policy
lessons.body:
## What to do

- List the never-enter items: passwords, bank details, medical records, other people's information
- Read one tool's privacy policy and find what it keeps
- Discuss: a free tool is paid for somehow

## Understand it

When you type into an online AI tool, your words travel to a company's computers. Depending on the service and its settings, they may be **stored**, **read by staff** reviewing quality, and **used to train future models**. Assume anything you type could be seen by someone else.

Things that must never go in the box:

- **Passwords, PINs, bank or card details** — ever.
- **Personal details** — your full name with your address, school, phone number or date of birth; and especially anybody else's.
- **Photos of people**, particularly children, without their permission.
- **Private information about others** — a friend's secrets, a family matter, someone's medical or school records.
- **Confidential work** — an organisation's internal documents, member lists, unpublished plans.

Safer habits:

- **Remove the details.** Instead of "My friend Kemi Bello at … School is being bullied by …", ask "How can I support a friend who is being bullied?"
- **Check the settings.** Many tools let you turn off saving history or training on your conversations.
- **Use approved tools** for school and NGG work, with an adult's guidance if you are under the tool's minimum age (often 13, sometimes 18).

Privacy is a right, and it is protected in Nigeria by the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023. Protecting other people's information is part of using these tools responsibly.

## Key words

- **Personal data:** information that identifies a person
- **Data retention:** how long a service keeps what you send it
- **Anonymise:** remove details that identify people

lessons.title: Schoolwork and honesty
lessons.summary: Where help ends and cheating begins, and how to tell the difference reliably.
objectives: You will state where the line is in your own words
You will declare assistance on a piece of work
You will explain work you submitted
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Agree the rule as a class: it may explain and check; it may not produce your work
- Practise declaring: what you asked, what you used
- Test: can you explain every line you submitted? If not, it is not yours

## Understand it

Schoolwork exists so that *you* learn. Using a tool to skip the learning is like sending someone else to the gym for you: the work gets done, but you do not get stronger.

A reliable test: **could you do it again, now, without the tool, and explain every part?** If yes, the tool helped you learn. If no, it did the learning for you.

Usually **help** (learning):

- Asking it to explain a concept a different way, then practising yourself.
- Asking for a practice question, answering it yourself, then checking.
- Checking spelling and grammar in writing you wrote.
- Brainstorming ideas that you then choose, develop and write yourself.

Usually **cheating** (or close to it):

- Copying its answer into homework or an exam.
- Asking it to write your essay, then changing a few words.
- Using it when your teacher said not to.
- Presenting its work as your own without saying you used it.

The rules differ between schools, teachers and tasks — **ask** when unsure, and **say** when you used a tool and how. Teachers increasingly can tell, but that is not the real reason: the exam, the job interview and real life will test what is in your head, not what is in the tool.

## Key words

- **Academic integrity:** honesty in learning and assessment
- **Plagiarism:** presenting someone else's work as your own
- **Disclosure:** saying openly which tools you used and how

objectives: You will train a classifier on your own examples

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Use Teachable Machine to train an image or sound classifier
- Test it on new examples and record the accuracy
- Deliberately find an input that fools it, and explain why

## Understand it

**Teachable Machine** lets you train a real image, sound or pose classifier in your browser, with no code.

1. **Choose classes** — the categories, such as *thumbs up*, *thumbs down*, *nothing*. Always include a "nothing / background" class, or the model must pick one of your gestures even when you do nothing.
2. **Collect examples** — record many images of each class with the webcam: different angles, distances, lighting and backgrounds. Aim for 100+ per class, balanced across classes.
3. **Train** — the tool learns to separate the classes.
4. **Test** — try it live. Then test it *properly*: new lighting, a different person, a different background, a partly hidden hand.

Now **find where it fails** — this is the real lesson. Typical failures:

- It learns the **background** or **your shirt colour** instead of the gesture, because those were the same in every example of one class.
- It works on you but not on a classmate with a different skin tone, because they were not in the data.
- It gives a confident answer to something it was never trained on.

Write down each failure and its likely cause, then improve the data and retrain. You will see directly that **the data matters more than the algorithm** — the same lesson professionals learn on systems costing millions.

Teachable Machine runs the training in your browser; still, do not record anybody without permission.

## Key words

- **Class:** one category a classifier chooses between
- **Balanced data:** a similar number of examples for each class
- **Overfitting:** learning the training examples too closely, including irrelevant details
- **Confidence score:** how strongly the model favours an answer — not how likely it is to be right

## What to do

- List local jobs and split the tasks: automatable, assisted, untouched
- Note what needs hands, presence, trust or accountability
- Discuss what to be good at

## Understand it

AI tools change *tasks* more than whole *jobs*. Most jobs are a bundle of tasks, and these systems are good at some and poor at others.

**Tasks they increasingly help with:** drafting routine text and emails, summarising long documents, translating between major languages, writing simple code, producing first-draft images, answering common customer questions, and sorting large amounts of data.

**Tasks they handle poorly:**

- Work needing **physical skill** in messy real places — electricians, nurses, mechanics, chefs, technicians who install and repair.
- Work built on **trust and relationships** — teaching, mentoring, caring, selling to people who know you, community leadership.
- **Judgement and responsibility** — deciding, being accountable, handling the unusual case.
- **Local knowledge** — Nigerian markets, languages, regulations and communities are poorly represented in the data.

What to build a career on:

1. **Deep skill in a real domain** — health, agriculture, engineering, law, design, business. The tool is most powerful in the hands of someone who knows the work.
2. **Using the tools well** — knowing when to use them and how to check them.
3. **Human skills** — communication, teamwork, leadership, creativity, ethics.
4. **Learning how to learn**, because tools will keep changing.

Nigeria's young population is an advantage: people who combine a real skill with confident, careful use of new tools will be in demand.

- **Automation:** machines doing tasks people used to do
- **Augmentation:** tools making people faster or better at their work

## What to do

- Demonstrate your classifier live
- Show the input that defeats it — the failures are the interesting part
- State one application of it you would refuse, and why

## Understand it

Presenting a model honestly is a professional skill. Engineers who build real systems publish **model cards**: short documents describing what a model is for, how it was trained, how well it works, where it fails, and what it must not be used for. Your presentation is a spoken model card.

Structure it like this:

1. **What it does** — the task and the classes. Demonstrate it working.
2. **The data** — how many examples of each class, how you collected them, who and what is in them, and who is not.
3. **How well it works** — test it on examples it has never seen and report how many it got right, for each class.
4. **Where it fails** — show at least two real failures live, and explain the likely cause (the background, the lighting, missing kinds of examples).
5. **What you changed** — what improved after you fixed the data.
6. **What it must NOT be used for** — be specific. A gesture classifier trained on twelve classmates must not be used to decide anything about anyone.

Showing failures openly is not a weakness. It is what makes others trust your work — and it is exactly what was missing in the real-world cases of bias you studied.

## Key words

- **Model card:** a short document describing a model's purpose, data, performance and limits
- **Accuracy:** the share of test examples the model got right
- **Intended use:** what a model is, and is not, suitable for

lessons.summary: You are a target because you are easy, not because you are important.
objectives: You will name three things of yours an attacker wants
You will say why ordinary people are targeted
You will list what you would lose
lessons.body:
## What to do

- List what you hold: accounts, contacts, photos, airtime, your name
- Learn that most attacks are automated and untargeted — they look for easy, not for valuable
- Write what you would actually lose if your main account went

## Understand it

Most cyber attacks are not aimed at anyone in particular. Criminals use automated tools to try millions of accounts, send millions of messages and scan millions of devices, then profit from whoever is easiest. You are a target not because you are important, but because **you have something worth taking and might be easy**.

What attackers want from ordinary people:

- **Money** — bank details, mobile money, airtime, card numbers.
- **Accounts** — a WhatsApp, Instagram or email account can be used to scam your contacts, who trust messages from you.
- **Your device** — to use its processing power, send spam, or spy.
- **Information** — personal details to sell, or to make the next scam more convincing.

The good news: because attackers look for the easy targets, a handful of habits puts you ahead of most people:

1. A different strong password for each important account, kept in a password manager.
2. Two-step verification on email, WhatsApp, social media and banking.
3. Updating your phone and apps promptly.
4. Stopping to think before clicking links or acting on urgent messages.
5. Backing up what matters.

This course takes each of these in turn. Security is not about being an expert — it is about not being the easy one.

## Key words

- **Attacker:** someone trying to gain access to systems or information without permission
- **Opportunistic attack:** an attack on whoever is easiest, not on a chosen person
- **Account takeover:** a criminal gaining control of someone's account

lessons.title: Passwords, properly
lessons.summary: Why reuse is the real danger, and how a manager fixes it.
objectives: You will explain why reusing a password is the main risk

You will set up a password manager
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Learn the chain: one site is breached, and every site with that password falls
- Build a passphrase: four unrelated words, long, memorable
- Set up a free password manager and move three accounts into it

## Understand it

The biggest password danger is not that yours is too short — it is **reuse**. Websites get breached all the time, and lists of stolen email-and-password pairs are sold and shared. Criminals then try those same pairs on email, banking and social media sites automatically (**credential stuffing**). If you use one password everywhere, one leak opens everything.

What makes a good password:

- **Long beats complicated.** Three random words — `orange-canoe-thunder` — is long, easy to remember and very hard to guess. `P@ssw0rd1` is short and in every attacker's list.
- **Unique** for every important account.
- **Never** your name, birthday, phone number, pet's name or football club.

Nobody can remember dozens of unique passwords, which is why security experts recommend a **password manager**: an app that creates and stores strong passwords for every site, locked behind one strong master password. Reputable ones include Bitwarden (free), and the managers built into Google, Apple and Microsoft accounts.

Check whether your email has appeared in a known breach at **Have I Been Pwned**. If it has, change that password — and every other account that used the same one.

And never share a password, even with a friend. A real company or bank will never ask you for it.

## Key words

- **Credential stuffing:** trying stolen username–password pairs on many sites
- **Password manager:** an app that creates, stores and fills strong passwords
- **Passphrase:** a password made of several random words
- **Data breach:** when a site's stored information is stolen

lessons.title: Two-factor authentication
lessons.summary: The second step that stops a stolen password being enough.
objectives: You will turn on 2FA for one real account
You will say why an app beats SMS
You will store recovery codes safely
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Turn on 2FA on your main account using an authenticator app
- Learn why SMS is weaker: a SIM can be swapped
- Save the recovery codes somewhere offline

## Understand it

**Two-step verification** (also called two-factor authentication, 2FA) means that logging in needs two different things: something you **know** (your password) and something you **have** (your phone) — so a stolen password alone is not enough.

The common second steps, from weakest to strongest:

1. **SMS codes** — a code texted to your phone. Much better than nothing, but vulnerable to SIM-swap fraud, where a criminal persuades a network to move your number to their SIM.
2. **Authenticator apps** — Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, or similar — generate a new six-digit code every 30 seconds on your phone. Stronger than SMS.
3. **Passkeys and security keys** — your phone's fingerprint or face unlock, or a physical key, confirm it is you. The strongest, and resistant to fake login pages.

Turn it on first for the accounts that unlock others: **email** (it resets every other password), then **WhatsApp** (Settings → Account → Two-step verification sets a PIN), banking, and social media.

Two rules make it work:

- **Never share a code.** Scammers often pretend to be friends or support staff: "I sent a code to your phone by mistake, please forward it." That code is the key to your account.
- **Save your backup codes** somewhere safe, so losing your phone does not lock you out for ever.

## Key words

- **Two-step verification (2FA):** a second proof of identity besides your password
- **Authenticator app:** an app that makes time-limited login codes
- **SIM swap:** fraud that moves your phone number to a criminal's SIM
- **Passkey:** a login using your device's fingerprint or face unlock instead of a password

## Read and watch

- [Turn on two-step verification](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/top-tips-for-staying-secure-online/activate-2-step-verification-on-your-email) — UK National Cyber Security Centre

1. Store your recovery codes where you will still have them if the phone is lost

lessons.title: Spotting phishing
lessons.summary: The messages that try to make you act before you think.
objectives: You will name five signs of a phishing message
You will check a link before following it
You will say why urgency is the main tool
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Examine real phishing messages and list the signs
- Check a link by reading the actual domain, not the text
- Notice how every one creates urgency

. **With an AI assistant —** paste the TEXT of a suspicious message — never a real account detail, never a password — and ask what the red flags are. Then verify the sender yourself through a number you already had.

## Understand it

**Phishing** is a message designed to trick you into giving away information, paying money or clicking something harmful. It arrives by email, SMS (smishing), WhatsApp or phone call (vishing).

Nearly every phishing message pushes the same emotional buttons, to make you act before you think:

- **Urgency** — "Your account will be closed in 24 hours."
- **Fear** — "Suspicious login detected. Verify now."
- **Greed or excitement** — "You have won ₦500,000. Claim now."
- **Authority** — pretending to be your bank, a government agency, a delivery company or your school.
- **Helpfulness** — a "friend" in trouble needing money or a code.

Warning signs:

- The sender's address or number does not match the real organisation (look closely: `zenithbank-verify.com` is not Zenith Bank).
- A link whose real destination (press and hold on a phone, hover on a laptop) is not the official site.
- Requests for passwords, PINs, BVN, OTP codes or card details — **legitimate organisations never ask for these**.
- Attachments you did not expect.

The fix is a habit: **stop, check, then act through a channel you already trust** — open the bank app yourself, call the number on the back of your card, or ask the friend on a call. Never use the link or number in the suspicious message.

## Key words

- **Phishing:** a fraudulent message designed to trick you
- **Smishing / vishing:** phishing by SMS / by voice call
- **Social engineering:** manipulating people rather than hacking computers
- **OTP:** one-time password — a code that must never be shared

lessons.summary: Nigerian-specific fraud: the patterns, and how to refuse them.
objectives: You will describe three scams common in Nigeria
You will say what they all have in common
You will state a refusal script
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Study real local patterns: fake job offers, POS fraud, romance scams, fake bank calls
- Find the common thread: urgency, authority, secrecy
- Agree a refusal: "I will call the official number back"

## Understand it

Some frauds are especially common in Nigeria. Knowing the patterns makes them easy to refuse.

- **Fake bank alerts.** A buyer "pays" you and shows an SMS or screenshot of a credit alert — but the money never arrives. Always confirm in your own banking app or with the bank before releasing goods.
- **BVN and account "updates".** A call or message claims your BVN or account needs updating or will be blocked, and asks for your BVN, card details, PIN or the OTP sent to your phone. Banks never ask for these.
- **Impersonated contacts.** A hacked WhatsApp account — or a new number with a familiar profile photo — messages your family: "I'm stranded, please send money urgently." Call the real person on their known number.
- **Fake jobs and scholarships.** Offers that require a "processing fee", or ask for your documents and account details up front.
- **Investment and "double your money" schemes** — including fake crypto platforms and Ponzi schemes. If returns are guaranteed and high, it is a scam.
- **POS and mobile-money tricks** — someone "accidentally" sends you money and asks for it back to a different account, or a vendor swaps your card.

lessons.title: Your devices
lessons.summary: Updates, lock screens and backups — the three that stop most of it.
objectives: You will update a device and say why it matters
You will set a lock screen
You will make a real backup
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Update one device fully and read what the update fixed
- Set a strong lock screen on your phone
- Back up photos and documents somewhere that survives losing the phone

## Understand it

Three habits stop most attacks on your devices.

**1. Update promptly.** Software has mistakes — **vulnerabilities** — that attackers learn to exploit. Updates fix them. Turn on automatic updates for your phone's operating system and apps, and install them soon after they arrive. An old phone that no longer receives security updates is a growing risk for banking and important accounts.

**2. Lock it.** Use a screen lock — a 6-digit PIN or longer, or fingerprint/face unlock with a PIN behind it. Patterns are easy to watch over your shoulder. Set the screen to lock after a short time. Turn on **Find My Device** (Android) or **Find My** (iPhone), so a lost phone can be located, locked or wiped.

**3. Back it up.** Phones get stolen, dropped and broken. Back up photos and documents to a cloud account (Google Photos, iCloud, OneDrive) and important chats (WhatsApp's own backup). Then losing the phone costs you a phone, not your memories and work.

Also:

- Install apps only from the official **Play Store** or **App Store**; apps from random links can contain malware.
- Review **app permissions** — a torch app does not need your contacts or microphone.
- Do not plug your phone into unknown USB ports or lend it unlocked.

## Key words

- **Vulnerability:** a flaw in software that an attacker can exploit
- **Patch / update:** a software fix for flaws
- **Malware:** software designed to cause harm
- **Remote wipe:** erasing a lost device from another device

## Read and watch

- [Device security guidance](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/top-tips-for-staying-secure-online/install-the-latest-software-and-app-updates) — UK National Cyber Security Centre

lessons.title: Phishing again, harder
lessons.summary: Returning to week 4 with the messages that actually fool trained people.
objectives: You will analyse harder phishing examples
You will find the one sign that still gives them away

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Examine well-made phishing with no spelling errors and a real-looking domain
- Find what still gives it away: the domain, the request, the channel
- Agree the rule that survives: verify through a channel they did not give you

## Understand it

Trained people get caught by phishing too — usually by the well-made, targeted kind. **Spear phishing** is aimed at one person or organisation, using real details to look genuine: your real name, your manager's name, a real project, a real supplier.

Harder techniques to know:

- **Look-alike addresses and domains**: `rn` instead of `m` (`ngg-adrnin.org`), a zero instead of an O, an extra word (`paystack-support.co`).
- **Compromised real accounts**: the message genuinely comes from a colleague's or friend's account, because it was hacked. The sender is right; the request is wrong.
- **Fake login pages** that look identical to the real one and even use HTTPS — the padlock only means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is honest.
- **Business email compromise**: an "urgent" message from the boss asking for a payment to new bank details, or for gift cards.
- **Multi-step stories** that build trust over days before the request arrives.

Defences that work against even good fakes:

- **Verify unusual requests through a second channel** — call the person on a number you already have.
- **Never change payment details on email alone.**
- **Type addresses yourself** or use bookmarks for important logins.
- Use **passkeys and password managers** — they will not fill a password into a fake site.
- **Report** suspicious messages; one report can protect a whole organisation.

## Key words

- **Spear phishing:** phishing targeted at a specific person using real details
- **Look-alike domain:** a web address made to resemble a real one
- **Business email compromise:** fraud using fake or hijacked work email to request payments

lessons.summary: What is already public about you, and what to do about it.
objectives: You will search for yourself and record what is public

## What to do

- Search your own name and record what is findable
- Tighten privacy settings on your most-used account
- Connect it: a birthday and a school name are security answers

## Understand it

Your **digital footprint** is everything about you that can be found online. Criminals use it to guess passwords and security answers and to make scams convincing; it also shapes what schools, employers and others think of you.

**Find out what is out there:**

- Search your full name in quotes, with your town or school, on a search engine and in image search.
- Look at your profiles while logged out, or ask a friend to look — what can a stranger see?
- Check **Have I Been Pwned** for breaches involving your email.

**Then reduce it:**

- Set social accounts to **private**, and review who follows you.
- Remove your **phone number, birthday, school and home area** from public profiles. Those details answer security questions and help scammers.
- Turn off **location** on posts and in your camera; stop posting where you are *while* you are there.
- Delete or archive old posts you would not want seen now.
- Review apps connected to your accounts and remove ones you no longer use.
- Ask friends to remove photos of you that you do not want online.

Think of it as **footprint management**: you cannot erase everything, but you can make yourself much harder to profile — and keep control of the story people find.

## Key words

- **Digital footprint:** everything about you that can be found online
- **OSINT:** open-source intelligence — information gathered from public sources
- **Oversharing:** posting personal details that can be misused

lessons.title: Networks you do not control
lessons.summary: Public Wi-Fi, shared computers and cyber cafés.
objectives: You will say what a stranger on the same network can see
You will check for HTTPS
You will use a shared computer safely
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Learn what is and is not visible on an open network
- Check for HTTPS before entering anything
- Rules for a shared machine: private window, log out, never save the password

## Understand it

On a network you do not control — café Wi-Fi, a hotel, a public hotspot, a shared office — you cannot be sure who else is watching or who runs it.

**Public Wi-Fi risks:**

- A criminal can set up a fake hotspot with a convincing name ("Airport_Free_WiFi") and see or tamper with traffic.
- On a poorly secured network, others may see which sites you visit.

Modern websites and apps use **HTTPS** encryption, which protects the content of most traffic. Still:

- Prefer your **mobile data** for banking and important logins.
- Only connect to networks you can confirm with staff, and "forget" them afterwards.
- Turn off automatic connection to open Wi-Fi.
- Never ignore browser warnings about certificates or insecure connections.

**Shared computers** (cyber cafés, school labs, library PCs) are riskier still: someone may have installed a **keylogger** that records everything typed.

- Avoid logging into banking or your main email on them at all.
- If you must log in, use a **private / incognito window**, never tick "remember me", and **sign out** fully at the end.
- Close the browser, and do not leave files in Downloads.
- Turn on login alerts, so you know if someone uses your account later.

If you think an account was used on an unsafe computer, change its password from a device you trust and sign out of all sessions.

## Key words

- **Public Wi-Fi:** a wireless network open to anyone
- **Evil twin:** a fake hotspot pretending to be a real one
- **HTTPS:** encrypted web connections, shown by the padlock
- **Keylogger:** software or hardware that records keystrokes

lessons.title: When it happens anyway
lessons.summary: The response: what to do first, second and third when an account is taken.
objectives: You will write a response plan in order
You will say what to do in the first ten minutes
You will know who to tell
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Write the order: change the password, revoke sessions, check recovery details, tell contacts, report
- Learn why revoking sessions matters — a password change alone may not log them out
- Identify who to report to: the platform, the bank, an adult

## Understand it

If an account is taken over, speed matters. Work in this order:

**First — stop the damage (within minutes).**

1. From a device you trust, try to log in and **change the password**. Use the service's "forgot password" if it was changed.
2. **Sign out all other sessions** (most services have this in security settings).
3. **Turn on two-step verification**, or reset it if the attacker changed it.
4. If money is involved, **call your bank immediately** using the number on your card or the official app, to freeze cards and accounts.

**Second — recover and secure (same day).**

5. Use the platform's official **account recovery** process (for WhatsApp, Instagram and email this is in their help centres). Never pay "recovery experts" who contact you — that is another scam.
6. Check and remove anything the attacker added: forwarding rules in email, new recovery numbers, linked devices, connected apps.
7. Change the password on **any other account that used the same password**.
8. **Warn your contacts** that messages from your account were not from you.

**Third — learn and report.**

9. Work out how it happened (phishing link? reused password? shared code?) and fix that habit.
10. **Report** to the platform, your bank, and the relevant authority. Keep screenshots as evidence.

It is not shameful to be hacked — it happens to experts. Hiding it helps only the attacker.

## Key words

- **Incident response:** the planned steps taken after a security problem
- **Session:** a logged-in connection that may stay active on a device
- **Account recovery:** a service's official process to regain a lost account

lessons.title: The law, and the line
lessons.summary: Testing anything you do not own is a crime, and what to do instead.
objectives: You will state what Nigerian law says about unauthorised access
You will describe responsible disclosure
You will name two legal places to practise
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Read about the Cybercrimes Act and what unauthorised access means
- Learn responsible disclosure: report privately, do not exploit, do not publish
- Find legal practice ranges and capture-the-flag sites

## Understand it

Security skills can protect or harm, and the law draws a clear line: **accessing, testing or interfering with a system you do not own, without permission, is a crime** — even if you "only wanted to see", even if you did no damage, and even if it was easy.

In Nigeria, the **Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act 2015** makes unauthorised access to computer systems, interception of communications, identity theft and computer-related fraud offences, with fines and prison terms. Many other countries have similar laws, and online crimes often cross borders.

Things that are **illegal without permission**: logging into someone else's account (even a friend's, even if they told you their password once); trying passwords on a site; scanning or attacking a network, website or school system; installing spyware on someone's phone; reading someone's private messages.

The legal ways to build real skills:

- **Capture the Flag (CTF)** competitions like **picoCTF**, designed for students, with puzzles you are allowed to attack.
- **Practice labs** made for learning, and your own devices and networks.
- **Bug bounty programmes**, where companies publicly invite testing under written rules (with age limits).
- If you find a real flaw by accident, **report it responsibly** to the owner and do not use or share it.

Ethical hackers are in high demand. The difference between them and criminals is permission.

## Key words

- **Unauthorised access:** using a computer system without the owner's permission
- **Ethical hacking:** authorised security testing to find and fix weaknesses
- **Capture the Flag (CTF):** legal security competitions with deliberate puzzles
- **Responsible disclosure:** privately reporting a flaw to its owner so it can be fixed

- [OWASP Foundation](https://owasp.org/) — OWASP Foundation

lessons.summary: Most of the work is reading, deciding and fixing. Writing new code is the small part.
objectives: You will describe how a developer spends a working day

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Discuss where the hours actually go: reading, meetings, debugging, testing, writing
- Install an editor and run one small program
- Learn the ratio — you will read far more code than you write

## Understand it

Films show programmers typing fast in the dark. Real software work looks different. Studies of professional developers find that they spend more time **reading code** than writing it, and a large share of their week on **understanding problems, fixing bugs, testing, reviewing each other's work and talking** to colleagues and users.

A typical change goes like this:

1. **Understand the problem.** What exactly is wrong or needed, for whom? Ask questions until it is clear.
2. **Read the existing code** to find where the change belongs and what it might affect.
3. **Decide** on an approach — often the smallest change that solves the problem safely.
4. **Write** the code — frequently only a few lines.
5. **Test** that it works and that nothing else broke.
6. **Get it reviewed** by a teammate.
7. **Ship it**, then watch that it behaves in real use.

So the skills that matter most are not typing speed or memorising syntax. They are: reading carefully, breaking problems into small pieces, asking good questions, testing your own work, explaining your decisions in writing, and staying calm when things break. Those are learnable — and they are what this course practises.

Software jobs exist in every sector — banks, telecoms, hospitals, farms, logistics, government — not only tech companies.

## Key words

- **Codebase:** all the code that makes up a piece of software
- **Maintenance:** changing and fixing existing software, which is most of the work
- **Code review:** a teammate reading your change before it is accepted

## Read and watch

- [Pro Git: about version control](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Getting-Started-About-Version-Control) — Pro Git book (git-scm.com)

lessons.summary: Git: saving your work in a way that lets you go back, and lets two people work at once.
objectives: You will commit changes with clear messages

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Init a repository, commit, and read the log
- Branch, change something, merge it back
- Delete a file and recover it from history

## Understand it

**Version control** records every change to a project, who made it and why, so you can go back to any earlier version and several people can work at once without overwriting each other. **Git** is the version control system almost every developer uses.

The core ideas:

- A **repository** (repo) is a project tracked by Git.
- A **commit** is a saved snapshot, with a message explaining the change.
- A **branch** is a separate line of work. You make a branch for a new feature, work on it without disturbing the main version, then **merge** it back when it is ready.

```bash
git init                       # start tracking a folder
git status                     # what has changed?
git add index.html             # stage a change for the next commit
git commit -m "Add sign-up form"
git switch -c fix-login        # make and move to a new branch
git log --oneline              # the history
```

Hosting services such as **GitHub** keep a copy of your repo online — a backup, and the place where teams share work.

Good habits: commit small, related changes together; write messages that say *what and why* ("Fix crash when the name is empty"); commit often; never commit passwords or keys.

## Key words

- **Repository:** a project whose history Git tracks
- **Commit:** a saved snapshot with a message
- **Branch:** a separate line of work that can later be merged
- **Merge:** combining the changes from one branch into another

## What to do

- Take an unfamiliar small project and find where it starts
- Trace one behaviour from the interface to the code that does it

## Understand it

Reading someone else's code is the skill developers use most — and it can be practised deliberately.

A method that works on any unfamiliar code:

1. **Start from the outside.** Read the README. What does the program do? How is it run? What are the main folders and files?
2. **Find the entry point** — where it starts (`index.html`, `main.py`, `server.js`, the function called first).
3. **Follow one path.** Pick one thing the program does — "what happens when I press Submit?" — and trace it from start to finish, file to file. Ignore everything else for now.
4. **Run it and experiment.** Change a value, add a `console.log` or `print`, and see what happens. Running code teaches more than staring at it.
5. **Name what you find.** Write short notes: "`validate()` checks the email, returns true or false". Draw a box diagram of which part calls which.
6. **Use the tools.** Your editor can *Go to definition* and *Find all references* — use them instead of scrolling.

When something is confusing, it may be badly written — that is useful information too. Notice what makes code *easy* to read (clear names, short functions, comments that explain *why*) and copy those habits in your own work.

## Key words

- **Entry point:** where a program starts running
- **Tracing:** following the path a program takes for one action
- **Go to definition:** an editor feature that jumps to where something is defined

lessons.title: Debugging
lessons.summary: Reproduce, isolate, fix, verify — in that order, every time.
objectives: You will reproduce a bug reliably
You will isolate it to a few lines
You will verify the fix actually fixed it
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Reproduce the bug on demand before changing anything
- Halve the search space repeatedly until you find it
- Fix, then verify by reproducing the original steps

. **With an AI assistant —** ask it to explain an error message line by line, then fix the bug yourself. Ask "why" until you could explain it to a classmate.

## Understand it

Debugging is a method, not luck. Professionals follow the same four steps every time:

1. **Reproduce.** Find exact steps that make the bug happen *every* time. "It sometimes crashes" cannot be fixed; "it crashes when the name field is empty and I press Save" can.
2. **Isolate.** Narrow down where it goes wrong. Read the error message and the line it points to. Print values (`console.log`, `print`) or use a debugger's breakpoints to compare what the code *actually* does with what you *expect*. Cut the problem in half repeatedly — is the data wrong before this function or after it?
3. **Fix** the cause, not the symptom. Hiding an error message is not a fix.
4. **Verify.** Repeat the original steps — it is fixed. Then check that nothing else broke.

Useful tactics:

- **Change one thing at a time**, so you know what made the difference.
- **Explain it out loud** to someone (or a rubber duck). Saying each step often reveals the wrong assumption.
- **Check the obvious** — is the file saved? Is the server restarted? Is it the right file?
- **Search the exact error message.** Someone has almost certainly met it before.
- **Take a break.** Fresh eyes find bugs that tired eyes miss.

Keep a short bug log: symptom, cause, fix. Patterns appear quickly.

## Key words

- **Reproduce:** make a bug happen reliably on purpose
- **Isolate:** narrow down where a bug is
- **Breakpoint:** a line where a debugger pauses the program
- **Root cause:** the underlying reason for a bug, not just its symptom

lessons.title: Your first test
lessons.summary: Why tests exist, and writing one that would have caught yesterday's bug.
objectives: You will write a test that fails, then make it pass
You will say what a test actually protects
You will test an edge case
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Write a failing test first, then the code that satisfies it
- Test the edge: empty, zero, very large, missing
- Learn what a test protects — the next person changing this code

## Understand it

A **test** is code that checks your code. You describe what *should* happen, and the computer checks it every time you run the tests:

```js
// grade.js
function grade(score) { return score >= 50 ? "Pass" : "Try again"; }
module.exports = grade;

// grade.test.js  (run with: npx jest)
const grade = require("./grade");
test("50 is a pass", () => { expect(grade(50)).toBe("Pass"); });
test("49 is not", () => { expect(grade(49)).toBe("Try again"); });
```

Why bother, when you can just try the program? Because:

- **Programs change.** A fix today can break something you tested by hand last month. Automated tests re-check everything in seconds.
- **They catch regressions** — old bugs coming back.
- **They document behaviour** — a test says exactly what the code promises.
- **They give confidence to change code** without fear.

Good tests are **small** (one behaviour each), **named** for what they check, and cover the **edges**: empty input, zero, the boundary (49 and 50), very large values, wrong types.

The best first test is one that would have caught a real bug you just fixed: write it, watch it fail on the old code, then pass on the fixed code.

## Key words

- **Unit test:** a small automated check of one piece of code
- **Assertion:** a statement of what must be true, like expect(x).toBe(y)
- **Regression:** a bug that returns after being fixed
- **Edge case:** an unusual input at the limits

## Read and watch

- [Getting started with Jest](https://jestjs.io/docs/getting-started) — Jest

## What to do

- Write an issue: what happens, what should happen, how to reproduce
- Open a pull request describing the change
- Review a classmate's PR with two specific, kind comments

## Understand it

Teams get code into a shared project safely with a standard workflow:

1. **Issue.** Work starts as an issue — a written description of a bug or feature, with steps to reproduce or what "done" means. Issues are tracked, assigned and discussed.
2. **Branch.** You create a branch for that one issue, so your unfinished work cannot break the main version.
3. **Commit** small, clear changes on the branch.
4. **Pull request (PR).** When ready, you open a PR asking to merge your branch. It shows exactly what changed, and its description explains what and why, and how you tested it.
5. **Review.** Teammates read the change, ask questions and suggest improvements. Automated tests usually run too.
6. **Merge.** Once approved and passing, the branch is merged into main.

Good reviewing is kind and specific: comment on the code, not the person; ask questions ("What happens if the list is empty?") rather than giving orders; say what is good too.

Good PRs are **small** — one issue, easy to review. A 2,000-line PR gets a quick "looks good" because nobody can really read it; a 50-line PR gets a real review.

## Key words

- **Issue:** a tracked description of a bug or task
- **Pull request:** a proposal to merge a branch, with discussion and review
- **Code review:** teammates reading and commenting on a change
- **main branch:** the shared, working version of the project

objectives: You will write a regression test for the week 4 bug

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Check out the code as it was before the week 4 fix
- Write a test and watch it fail there
- Apply the fix and watch it pass

## Understand it

In week 4 you fixed a bug. Today you make sure it can never come back without someone noticing. This is called a **regression test**, and it is one of the most valuable habits in software.

The method:

1. **Write the test first**, describing the correct behaviour in the exact situation that used to fail.
2. **Prove the test works** by temporarily putting the bug back (or checking out the old version). The test must **fail**. A test that passes on broken code tests nothing.
3. **Restore the fix.** The test passes.
4. **Commit the test with the fix**, so they travel together.

```js
test("saving with an empty name shows an error instead of crashing", () => {
  expect(() => save({ name: "" })).not.toThrow();
  expect(save({ name: "" }).error).toBe("name_required");
});
```

Now look for the bug's relatives: if an empty name crashed, what about a name that is only spaces, or very long, or missing entirely? Add tests for those edges too.

Over time, a project's tests become a record of every mistake it has learnt from. That is why experienced teams insist that every bug fix arrives with a test.

## Key words

- **Regression test:** a test that stops a fixed bug from silently returning
- **Red–green:** watching a test fail on broken code, then pass on fixed code

## What to do

- Design a table for something real: students, stock, attendance
- Insert rows and query them back
- Try a bad design and feel the queries get hard

## Understand it

Variables vanish when a program stops. To keep data, programs use a **database**. The most common kind is **relational**: data lives in **tables** of **rows** (records) and **columns** (fields), like a strict spreadsheet.

```sql
CREATE TABLE learners (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  centre TEXT,
  age INTEGER
);
INSERT INTO learners (name, centre, age) VALUES ('Kemi', 'Egbeda', 13);
SELECT name, age FROM learners WHERE centre = 'Egbeda' ORDER BY name;
UPDATE learners SET age = 14 WHERE id = 1;
DELETE FROM learners WHERE id = 1;
```

That language is **SQL**. The four statements match the four things apps do to data: create, read, update, delete.

Key ideas:

- Every row has a unique **primary key** (`id`), so it can be found exactly.
- Each column has a **type** and rules (`NOT NULL`), so bad data is refused.
- Related tables link through ids — an `attendance` table stores `learner_id` rather than copying the name.

Never build a query by pasting user input into SQL text; use your library's **parameters** (`WHERE name = ?`). Pasting text in is how **SQL injection** attacks happen.

**SQLite** is a small, free database stored in a single file — ideal for learning.

## Key words

- **Table / row / column:** how relational data is organised
- **SQL:** the language for querying relational databases
- **Primary key:** a unique id for each row
- **SQL injection:** an attack that sneaks commands in through unescaped input

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Call a free public API and display part of the response
- Break it on purpose — wrong URL, no network — and handle it
- Check the response shape before using it

## Understand it

An **API** (application programming interface) is how one program asks another for data or actions. On the web, that usually means sending an **HTTP request** to a URL and getting back **JSON**.

```js
async function getCountry(name) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://restcountries.com/v3.1/name/${encodeURIComponent(name)}`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Request failed: ${res.status}`);
  const data = await res.json();
  return { name: data[0].name.common, capital: data[0].capital?.[0] };
}
```

The parts of working with any API:

1. **Read the documentation** — the URL, the parameters, what the response looks like, any limits.
2. **Make the request**, often with a key that identifies you.
3. **Check the status** — 2xx success, 4xx you asked wrongly, 5xx their server failed.
4. **Read the response** and take only what you need.
5. **Handle failure.** Networks drop, services go down, rate limits are hit. Your program must say something useful and recover — never crash or hang.

API keys are secrets: never commit them to a public repository or put them in front-end code anyone can read.

## Key words

- **API:** a defined way for programs to talk to each other
- **Endpoint:** a specific URL an API answers on
- **JSON:** the text format most APIs return
- **Rate limit:** how many requests an API allows in a period

## Read and watch

## What to do

- Deploy to a free host and get a public URL
- Open it on a phone on mobile data, not your Wi-Fi
- Learn why "it works on my machine" is not a defence

## Understand it

Software on your laptop helps only you. **Deployment** puts it on a computer that is always on and reachable, so others can use it.

What you deploy decides where:

- **Static sites** (HTML, CSS, front-end JavaScript only): free hosts such as **GitHub Pages** serve the files directly.
- **Server applications** (Node, Python, a database): an application host runs your program continuously; many have free tiers for learning.

The usual steps:

1. Code in a Git repository, without secrets.
2. Connect the repository to the host.
3. Tell it how to **build** and **start** your app.
4. Set **environment variables** (database address, keys) in the host's settings — never in the code.
5. Deploy, then **test the live version**, not just your local one.

Things that differ between "works on my machine" and live: file paths and their capital letters, the port number, missing environment variables, a database the host cannot reach, and slower networks.

Many teams set up **continuous deployment**: every merge to main runs the tests and, if they pass, deploys automatically. It makes releases small, frequent and boring — which is exactly what you want.

## Key words

- **Deployment:** putting software where its users can reach it
- **Static site:** a site of fixed files with no server-side program
- **Environment variable:** configuration given to a program from outside its code
- **Continuous deployment:** automatically releasing every tested change

## What to do

- Write the README: what it is, how to run it, how to contribute
- Give it to a classmate and watch them follow it without helping
- Fix every place they got stuck

## Understand it

Code that only its author understands has a short life. Two kinds of writing keep it alive.

**The README** is the front door of a project. A good one lets a stranger use it without asking you anything:

- **What it is** and who it is for, in two sentences — with a screenshot.
- **How to install and run it**, step by step, with the exact commands.
- **Configuration** — which environment variables are needed (with example values, never real secrets).
- **How to run the tests.**
- **How to contribute** and who to contact.

Test your README by giving it to a classmate and watching them follow it without help. Every question they ask is a missing line.

**Commit messages** explain each change for the future reader — often you, months later, trying to understand why something is the way it is. A well-known convention:

- A short **summary line** (about 50 characters) in the imperative: "Fix crash when the name is empty" — as if completing "This commit will…".
- A blank line, then a **body** explaining *why* the change was needed and anything surprising.

"fix", "stuff" and "update" tell nobody anything. History is only useful if it can be read.

## Key words

- **README:** the document that explains a project and how to use it
- **Commit message:** the explanation attached to a commit
- **Documentation:** written explanation of how software works and is used

## What to do

"Ship it" means a small application that a stranger could find, use, trust and maintain. Bring together the whole course:

lessons.title: Sense, think, act
lessons.summary: The three things every robot does, and spotting them in machines you already use.
objectives: You will name the three stages of a robot
You will identify them in three real machines
You will draw the loop for one
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Learn sense, think, act — and that it repeats as a loop
- Find them in a washing machine, a phone, a traffic light
- Draw the loop for one machine

## Understand it

Every robot, from a vacuum cleaner to a Mars rover, does three things in a loop:

1. **Sense** — measure the world with **sensors**: buttons, light sensors, distance sensors, cameras, temperature sensors, wheel encoders.
2. **Think** — a **controller** (a small computer) runs a program that decides what to do with those measurements.
3. **Act** — **actuators** change the world: motors turn wheels, servos move arms, speakers beep, lights glow.

Then it senses again and adjusts. That loop runs many times a second.

You already use sense-think-act machines:

- An **automatic door** senses a person (infrared), decides to open, and drives a motor.
- A **phone** rotates the screen when its accelerometer senses it turning.
- A **traffic light** with a camera or a road sensor changes timing depending on traffic.
- A **thermostat** or an **inverter** senses battery level and switches power sources.

A machine with no sensing — a toy that drives straight until it hits a wall — is not really a robot; it cannot react. The more a machine senses and adapts, the more "robotic" it is.

For each machine you look at this week, name its sensors, its controller and its actuators. That habit makes any robot understandable.

## Key words

- **Sensor:** a device that measures something in the world
- **Controller:** the computer that runs the robot's program
- **Actuator:** a device that makes something happen, like a motor
- **Feedback loop:** sensing, deciding and acting repeatedly

## Read and watch

- [Arduino: learn](https://docs.arduino.cc/learn/) — Arduino
- [Electrical engineering](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/electrical-engineering) — Khan Academy

1. Write what each one senses and what it does about it

lessons.title: Electricity, safely
lessons.summary: Voltage, current, and the rules that stop you destroying components or yourself.
objectives: You will explain voltage and current in your own words
You will check polarity before connecting
You will state the rule about mains electricity
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Voltage pushes, current flows — use the water analogy
- Check polarity every time; backwards kills components
- Learn the rule: we work on batteries only, never mains

## Understand it

Three quantities describe every circuit:

- **Voltage (V, volts)** — the "push" that drives electricity, like water pressure. A phone battery is about 3.7 V; an Arduino runs at 5 V; a USB port gives 5 V; mains in Nigeria is 230 V.
- **Current (I, amps)** — how much electricity flows, like the flow of water. Small parts use milliamps (mA).
- **Resistance (R, ohms Ω)** — how much something resists the flow, like a narrow pipe.

They are linked by **Ohm's law**: **V = I × R**. If you know two, you can work out the third. For example, 5 V across 250 Ω lets 0.02 A (20 mA) flow.

Safety rules for this course:

- **Never work with mains (230 V) electricity.** It can kill. Our projects use batteries and USB only.
- **Never short-circuit a battery** (connect + directly to −). Huge current flows; wires get hot, batteries can swell, burn or explode — lithium batteries especially.
- **Power off before changing wiring.**
- Check **polarity** — some parts (LEDs, electrolytic capacitors, batteries) only work one way round and can be destroyed backwards.
- If anything gets **hot, smells or smokes**, disconnect power immediately.

Respect the rules and these projects are completely safe.

## Key words

- **Voltage:** the electrical push, in volts
- **Current:** the flow of electricity, in amps
- **Resistance:** opposition to current, in ohms
- **Ohm's law:** V = I × R
- **Short circuit:** a path with almost no resistance, causing dangerous current

## Read and watch

- [What is a circuit?](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/what-is-a-circuit) — SparkFun Electronics

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Build it in Tinkercad first, then for real
- Work out the resistor value from the supply and the LED
- Learn what happens without a resistor — try it in simulation only

## Understand it

Your first circuit: a battery or 5 V supply, a **resistor** and an **LED** (light-emitting diode), connected in a loop on a **breadboard**.

**The breadboard** lets you build without soldering. Holes in each short row of five are connected underneath; the long rails along the edges are usually for power (+) and ground (−). Check the rails on your board — some are split in the middle.

**The LED** only lets current flow one way. Its longer leg (**anode**) goes towards +; the shorter leg (**cathode**, by the flat edge) towards −. Backwards, it simply stays dark.

**Why the resistor is not optional:** an LED has almost no resistance once it lights, so without a resistor the current shoots up and the LED burns out — and can damage the board powering it. The resistor limits the current.

Working it out with Ohm's law: a red LED drops about 2 V and is happy at about 15–20 mA. From a 5 V supply, the resistor has 5 − 2 = 3 V across it. R = V ÷ I = 3 ÷ 0.015 = 200 Ω. Use the next standard value up — **220 Ω** is the classic choice.

Read resistor colour bands (or measure with a multimeter): red-red-brown is 220 Ω.

If it does not light: check LED direction, check every connection is in the right row, check the power rails.

## Key words

- **Breadboard:** a board for building circuits without soldering
- **LED:** a light that only lets current flow one way
- **Anode / cathode:** the positive / negative leg of an LED
- **Current-limiting resistor:** a resistor that keeps current safe for a part

## What to do

- Connect a micro:bit or Arduino and upload a blink program
- Change the timing and upload again
- Break it deliberately and read the error

. **With an AI assistant —** ask it to explain an upload or compile error, then check what it says against the board's own documentation before you change any wiring.

## Understand it

A **microcontroller** is a tiny, cheap computer on a single chip, made to control things. An **Arduino Uno** is a board built around one, with pins you can connect to sensors and actuators, and a USB port to program it.

Every Arduino program (a **sketch**) has two parts:

```cpp
void setup() {
  pinMode(13, OUTPUT);        // runs once, at the start
}

void loop() {                 // runs again and again, for ever
  digitalWrite(13, HIGH);     // 5 V on pin 13: LED on
  delay(500);                 // wait 500 milliseconds
  digitalWrite(13, LOW);      // 0 V: LED off
  delay(500);
}
```

This is **Blink**, the "hello world" of electronics. Pin 13 has a small LED built onto the board, so it works with nothing connected.

The workflow: write the sketch in the **Arduino IDE** (or the online editor), choose your board and port, press **Upload**. The code is compiled and copied into the microcontroller, which then runs it on its own — even unplugged from the computer if it has another power source.

If you do not have a board yet, simulators such as **Wokwi** or **Tinkercad Circuits** run Arduino code in the browser.

Change the delays and watch the blink change: you are now programming hardware.

## Key words

- **Microcontroller:** a small computer on one chip, made for control tasks
- **Sketch:** an Arduino program
- **Pin:** a connection point on the board
- **Upload:** copy a compiled program onto the board

lessons.summary: Buttons and sensors: letting the world change what the program does.
objectives: You will read a button in code
You will read an analogue sensor value

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Read a button and act on it
- Read a light or distance sensor and print the values
- Watch the values wobble — real sensors are noisy

## Understand it

**Inputs** let the world change what a program does.

**A button** is a **digital** input: pressed or not, HIGH or LOW.

```cpp
const int BUTTON = 2, LED = 13;
void setup() { pinMode(BUTTON, INPUT_PULLUP); pinMode(LED, OUTPUT); }
void loop() {
  bool pressed = digitalRead(BUTTON) == LOW;   // pull-up: pressed reads LOW
  digitalWrite(LED, pressed ? HIGH : LOW);
}
```

`INPUT_PULLUP` turns on a resistor inside the chip that holds the pin HIGH until the button connects it to ground. Without it, an unconnected pin "floats" and reads random values — a classic bug.

Buttons also **bounce**: the metal contacts chatter for a few milliseconds, so one press can register as several. A short delay or checking the state twice solves it.

**Many sensors are analogue**: they give a voltage that varies, which `analogRead(A0)` turns into a number from **0 to 1023**. A **light-dependent resistor (LDR)** in a voltage divider, or a **potentiometer** (knob), are good first analogue inputs.

```cpp
int light = analogRead(A0);
Serial.println(light);   // watch the values in the Serial Monitor
```

Always print raw sensor values first and watch how they change before writing logic around them. Real sensors are noisy, and their numbers are rarely what you guessed.

## Key words

- **Digital input:** an input that is either on or off
- **Analogue input:** an input with a range of values
- **Pull-up resistor:** keeps an input pin at a known level when nothing is connected
- **Debouncing:** ignoring the rapid flicker of a button's contacts

## Understand it

**Outputs** make things happen — and motors are where robots become physical.

- **DC motors** spin continuously. Speed depends on voltage; reverse the wires and they spin the other way. Used for wheels.
- **Servo motors** turn to a set **angle** (usually 0–180°) and hold it. Used for steering, arms and grippers.
- **Stepper motors** move in precise steps. Used in 3D printers.

**Why motors need their own power:** an Arduino pin can safely supply only about 20 mA. A small motor can draw hundreds of milliamps, and much more when starting or stalled. Connected directly, it can reset or damage the board. So:

- Drive DC motors through a **motor driver** board (such as an L298N or a TB6612), which switches a separate battery's power under the Arduino's control and lets you reverse direction.
- Power servos from a separate supply where possible, and **connect all the grounds together** — the Arduino, the driver and the motor battery must share ground, or signals make no sense.

```cpp
#include <Servo.h>
Servo arm;
void setup() { arm.attach(9); }
void loop() { arm.write(0); delay(1000); arm.write(90); delay(1000); }
```

**PWM** (pulse-width modulation) — switching power on and off very fast — lets a pin control motor speed and LED brightness with `analogWrite()`.

## Key words

- **DC motor:** a motor that spins continuously
- **Servo:** a motor that moves to and holds an angle
- **Motor driver:** a circuit that powers motors under a controller's command
- **Common ground:** connecting the negative side of every power source together
- **PWM:** rapid on-off switching used to control speed or brightness
